Harish bhaiya,
It went exactly how I said it would. You kept telling me to prepare, but they were always going to pick someone from a big design school. So I looked at my portfolio once on Sunday and went to sleep at two anyway, because I couldn't stop thinking about it.

'We'll let you know.' We both know what that means.
So there it is. I was right. You'll say I didn't prepare, and fine, I didn't, but what was the point if the result was fixed?
Tell Ma I'll call on the weekend.
Parul

Why spend three evenings on it? I watched that cooking show instead and told myself I'd 'wing it'. Morning of, my hands were so cold I had to hold my tea glass for five minutes. They gave me Class 6, fractions. I'd been thinking of doing pizzas on the board, but I hadn't drawn one before, and it came out like an egg. The kids laughed. Then the principal asked how I'd help a child who was falling behind, and my mind went white. I said 'extra worksheets'. That's it. Two words. And I thought, see, Vandana, this is what always happens. I'm just not an interview person. Why are you looking at me like that?

passage: I'm Sabina, and I share a flat with Bhupen. The week before his bank interview, I kept offering to do mock questions with him. 'No point,' he said every time. 'They'll take someone with better marks.' He spent Wednesday rearranging his bookshelf. Thursday he played cricket videos till late. The night before, he ironed his shirt at one in the morning and kept saying, 'It's already gone, I can feel it.' I can't know exactly what was in his head. I only know he left without breakfast and his tie was crooked. He came back at noon and dropped onto the sofa. 'They asked about current rates and I blanked,' he said. 'Told you. I knew it.' He looked almost relieved, like being right was the one good thing about the day. I wanted to say he never gave himself a chance, but I just made him tea.

qa.q: What did Bhupen spend Wednesday doing?
qa.a: He spent Wednesday rearranging his bookshelf.

qa.q: Why might Bhupen have looked almost relieved after the interview?
qa.a: He had been so sure it would go badly that being proved right felt like the one good thing, a kind of comfort in the fear coming true.

qa.q: What could Bhupen have done differently when Sabina offered mock questions?
qa.a: He could have accepted the mock questions and prepared for topics like current rates, instead of spending the week on bookshelves and cricket videos.

qa.q: How does Sabina see what happened to Bhupen?
qa.a: Sabina thinks he never gave himself a chance, because his certainty of failing kept him from preparing, but Sabina chooses kindness and makes him tea instead of saying it.

grounding: A flatmate watches a young man who expects to fail a bank interview avoid preparation, arrive rattled and blank, then call it proof.

Monday. Darshan got the call: interview on Thursday, junior analyst. "They'll grill me on statistics and I'll blank," he told Kishore over dinner. Kishore offered to run practice questions with him. "Pointless. Either I know it or I don't." He watched a cricket match instead.
Thursday. In the waiting room his palms were wet. When the panel asked about regression, he heard himself say, "Sorry, I'm not good at this part," before he'd even tried. He stumbled through the case study he had never looked at, avoiding their eyes.
Saturday. The rejection email came. "See?" he told Kishore, almost relieved. "Knew it." Kishore didn't argue. He only asked, "How many practice questions did you do?" Darshan opened his mouth, then shut it.

qa.q: What did Darshan do instead of practice questions?
qa.a: He watched a cricket match.

qa.q: Why did Darshan feel almost relieved on Saturday?
qa.a: The rejection matched his prediction, so it felt like proof he had been right rather than something he had helped cause.

qa.q: Where was the real turning point, and what could Darshan have chosen then?
qa.a: On Monday, when Kishore offered practice questions; saying yes, even for an hour on regression, might have changed Thursday.

qa.q: Why might Kishore ask a question instead of arguing?
qa.a: Kishore likely saw that the fear had shaped the preparation, and a question lets Darshan notice it himself instead of feeling lectured.

grounding: A young adult sure an interview will go badly skips preparation, freezes in the room, and takes the rejection as proof he was right.

subtype: Predicting failure and drifting into it [Actor]
passage: Kamal, you keep saying the interview will be a disaster. Sit down; your Ishita Bua has a confession. In 1998 I was twenty-four and got a call for an announcer's job at the radio station. I was certain they wanted someone polished, someone from the city. So I didn't practise reading aloud even once. Why bother? The night before, I barely slept, sure of the ending. In the booth my voice shook so badly I lost my place twice. They were kind. They didn't take me. And I went home and told everyone, "I told you so," as if I'd won something. Two years later the same station called me again. That time I read the news aloud to your grandfather every night for a month. I got it. Same girl, same voice. The only thing that changed was what I did with the fear.

qa.q: What job was Ishita called for in 1998?
qa.a: An announcer's job at the radio station.

qa.q: What did Ishita do differently the second time, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Ishita read the news aloud every night for a month, preparing instead of predicting, which gave a steadier voice in the booth.

qa.q: How might Kamal hear "Same girl, same voice"?
qa.a: Kamal may realise the difference was preparation, not talent, so the coming interview is not already decided.

grounding: An elder recalls being sure an interview would fail, skipping practice, shaking in the booth and taking the rejection as proof, before preparing properly years later.
